extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and educated public interested in political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles from Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations on the nature of stock lent at interest, determinants of the rate of interest, legal regulation of usury, and the relative social value of different employments of capital (agriculture, manufacture, wholesale trade, retail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of spending type on public opulence
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes two species of expense: spending revenue in hospitality (sharing with friends and companions) versus purchasing durable commodities (often consumed by the spender).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hospitality shares revenue and is more favorable to public opulence; buying durable commodities often accumulates valuable goods and is more favorable to private frugality and increase of public capital. Spending on frivolous durable objects (ornaments, jewelry, gew-gaws) indicates a trifling and selfish disposition and is less conducive to growth of public opulence because it maintains unproductive rather than productive hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock lent at interest is capital with expectation of repayment
rubrics_metrics.description: The stock which is lent at interest is always considered as a capital by the lender: he expects restoration and certain annual rent (interest) during the loan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowers may use loaned stock either as capital (employing productive labourers who reproduce value with profit) or as stock for immediate consumption. Using it as consumption is prodigal and typically ruins borrower and lender. Lending for consumption is contrary to both parties' interest (except where gross usury is concerned).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loans as assignment of a portion of annual produce (money's worth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though loans are usually made in money (coin or paper), what the borrower really wants and the lender supplies is the money’s worth, i.e., the goods it can purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loaned money is effectively an assignment of a portion of the annual produce of land and labour to the borrower for use; money itself is merely the deed of assignment and different from what is assigned. The same pieces of money can successively serve as instruments of many loans and purchases, so the stock lent exceeds the literal amount of coins used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of stock lent is determined by part of annual produce reserved for replacing capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of stock (money) which can be lent at interest in any country is regulated by the value of that part of the annual produce destined for replacing capital and which the owner does not wish to employ himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not regulated by the nominal value or quantity of money (coin or paper) circulating, but by the real value of goods destined to replace capital and be lent out as income by their owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase in available capital reduces the rate of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: As the quantity of stock to be lent at interest increases, the interest (price for its use) necessarily diminishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two mechanisms: (1) General market effect — price falls as quantity increases; (2) competition among capitals — as capital increases, profits from employing new capital diminish, owners compete for employments, often by more reasonable terms, which lowers profits and thereby the rate of interest. Also competition raises wages and sinks profits, reducing interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy refutation: money supply increase alone doesn't lower interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase in gold and silver (money supply) without change in commodities cannot by itself lower the real rate of interest; lowering metal value affects nominal values equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith follows Hume in arguing that if metal value falls proportionally, the relation between capital and interest remains unchanged; reducing nominal metal value alone changes nominal prices but not real returns, so cannot explain observed long-term fall in interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase in commodity circulation relative to money augments real capital and lowers profits
rubrics_metrics.description: If quantity of commodities circulated increases while money remains the same, the country's capital is really augmented even if nominal money expression unchanged; it commands more labour and raises demand for labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This increases wages (in real terms) and diminishes profits of stock (both really and nominally), so the interest of money, which follows profits of stock, may be greatly diminished even as the apparent value of money rises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of interest increases usury
rubrics_metrics.description: Where interest is prohibited by law, the regulation tends to increase the evil of usury rather than prevent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because something can be made by using money, something ought to be paid; prohibition forces debtors to effectively insure creditors against penalties of usury, producing hidden or higher costs and illegal evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal rate of interest should be somewhat above lowest market rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws fixing the highest permissible rate of interest should set that rate somewhat above the lowest market price (the rate paid by those with best security).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If legal rate is below lowest market rate it mimics prohibition; if fixed precisely at lowest market rate it ruins credit for those without best security and forces them to usurers; if set far above lowest market rate it attracts risky borrowers (prodigals, projectors) and misallocates capital. Thus an appropriate legal rate should be slightly above the lowest market rate to favor sober borrowers and safe allocation of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal rate influences allocation of capital between borrowers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the legal rate is too high, much capital will be lent to prodigals and projectors; if appropriately set slightly above market low, sober people are preferred borrowers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High legal rates keep capital out of hands likely to be employed profitably, throwing it into hands likely to waste it; a rate only a little above the lowest market rate encourages lending to those most likely to use capital advantageously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary market price of land depends on ordinary market rate of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The market price of land everywhere depends upon the ordinary market rate of interest because owners deliberate between buying land or lending out capital at interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages of land (security and other benefits) compensate for lower revenue than lending; the balance determines typical years-purchase. Historical example: when interest 10% land sold at 10–12 years purchase; as interest fell to 6–5–4% land rose to 20–30 years purchase. Thus market interest shapes land valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals have four employments
rubrics_metrics.description: A capital may be employed in four ways: (1) procuring rude produce for consumption, (2) manufacturing and preparing rude produce, (3) transporting rude or manufactured produce, (4) dividing particular portions into small parcels for demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponding actors: farmers/miners/fishermen (first), master manufacturers (second), wholesale merchants (third), retailers (four). Each class is essential to existence or extension of the others and to general convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of each capital employment for the others
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the four methods of employing a capital is essentially necessary either to existence or extension of the other three, or to general convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: without capital for raw produce, manufactures/trade can't exist; without manufacturing capital, some raw produce would be worthless; without transport, production limited to neighbourhood; without division into parcels, consumers (especially poor) would face impractical bulk purchases and misallocate capital to consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retail trade enables small-scale consumption and productive capital use
rubrics_metrics.description: Retailers break down goods into small parcels, allowing poor workers to purchase subsistence in small quantities, enabling them to employ almost their whole stock as capital rather than tying it up in food stores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convenience allows small workmen to furnish more work and earn profits that compensate the retailer's margin; prejudices against shopkeepers are unfounded; multiple retailers increase competition benefiting consumers and producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retail and wholesale competition benefits consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition among retailers tends to make them sell cheaper and buy dearer, and dividing capital among many retailers reduces chances of collusion to raise prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if competition ruins some retailers, that is their business; the public benefit from lower prices and better access outweighs retailer losses. The alleged harm of many retailers (e.g., alehouses) causing social vices is misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons whose capitals are employed in these ways are productive labourers
rubrics_metrics.description: The persons (retailer, merchant, manufacturer, farmer) whose capitals are employed in the four ways are themselves productive labourers: their labour realizes itself in vendible commodities and adds value at least equal to their maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profits of these operators are drawn from the price of goods produced or traded. However, equal capitals in different employments mobilize different quantities of productive labour and add different amounts to annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different employments vary in productive labour mobilized and value added
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal capitals employed in retailing, wholesaling, manufacturing, and agriculture will immediately put into motion very different quantities of productive labour and augment the annual produce by different amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking and explanation: retailer employs the least immediate productive labour (mostly his own); wholesale merchant's capital replaces capitals of farmers/manufacturers and employs carriers; master manufacturer employs many workmen and uses fixed capital—thus puts more labour into motion; farmer employs most productive labour including labouring cattle and nature itself contributing free labour, often reproducing landlord's rent as an extra return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural capital is most advantageous to society
rubrics_metrics.description: No equal capital puts into motion a greater quantity of productive labour than that of the farmer; agriculture benefits from Nature's labour and often reproduces the landlord's rent, so agriculture adds more value to the annual produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agricultural operations both direct and augment nature's fertility; in agriculture a substantial portion of produce (rent) is due to nature rather than human labour. Consequently, per unit of capital employed, agriculture contributes more to real wealth and revenue than manufacture or trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residence/mobility of capital differs by employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals employed in agriculture and retail trade must generally reside within the society; wholesale merchant capital is mobile and can wander to buy cheap and sell dear; manufacturer capital must reside where the manufacture is carried on but that location is sometimes remote from materials or markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: domestic residence of certain capitals affects local employment and value added; some manufacturers can be useful to producing countries even if capital resides abroad (e.g., British manufacturers working Baltic flax), because they replace producers' capitals and encourage production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality of merchant's capital has limited importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the merchant exporting a society’s surplus produce is native or foreign is of little importance: a foreign merchant's capital gives value to their surplus produce by exchanging it for something demanded at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foreign merchant still replaces the capital of the producer and enables continued production; only the profits of the merchant (one man's share) differ in nationality, which has minor effect on total productive labour supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of having manufacturer capital reside domestically
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of consequence that manufacturer capital should reside within the country because it mobilizes more productive labour and adds more value to annual produce than capital that does not reside there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nevertheless, foreign manufacture of a country's raw materials can still be useful to that producing country because exporters replace the producer's capital and sustain production by creating demand abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: A country may lack sufficient capital for all employments
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular country may not have capital sufficient both to improve and cultivate all its lands, to manufacture all its produce, and to transport its surplus to distant markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constraint implies limits on domestic improvement and manufacture and helps explain trade patterns and the role of foreign capital or specialization.
